newsitem.title: CONGO: Talks start in Congo Brazzaville, gunfire continues.
newsitem.headline: Talks start in Congo Brazzaville, gunfire continues.

text.p: Congolese political leaders began contacts in Brazzaville on Sunday to try to end four days of fighting between the army and a political militia after a ceasefire call from the prime minister went unheeded.
Officials at the presidency said discussions began with representatives of ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso and other political leaders.

"We've already got somewhere with the political leaders, but we are having trouble getting the message across on the ground, the thing is now for the soldiers to calm down," said one senior official. "Some discussions have started."
He said a mediation committee would be chaired by Bernard Kolelas, the mayor of Brazzaville and President Pascal Lissouba's main political opponent.
It would include people from Lissouba's, Sassou Nguesso's and Kolelas's political factions as well as members of civic groups, he said. He said Lissouba was at the presidency.
Kolelas, whose supporters have played no part in the fighting so far, offered his mediation on Saturday.
A French soldier was shot dead and five others wounded in a firefight with unruly troops on Saturday as they evacuated foreign residents who had been trapped in a building by gunfire.
Witnesses said fighting was heavy overnight, particularly around the airport, and shooting could be heard in the town centre on Sunday.

"The problem is that there are Nguesso's militias and there are Congolese army units which are not under the control of their officers, and so we have seen Congolese troops firing on their fellow soldiers," said Commander Alexis Jaraud, the commander of French forces in the country.
"There is shooting in the streets, and they are using rocket-launchers in residential neighbourhoods," Jaraud told French television LCI by telephone.

The battles pitting followers of Sassou Nguesso against troops loyal to Lissouba began on Thursday after troops surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home to enforce a ban on private militias in the runup to July 27 presidential elections.
Lissouba's prime minister, Charles David Ganao, told state radio on Saturday night the polls would go ahead as planned and called for a halt to fighting and looting in the city.
There was no reliable death toll for the clashes although police sources spoke of several dozen dead and many wounded.
A plane carrying 44 U.S. citizens across the Congo River from Brazzaville to Kinshasa, the capital of Laurent Kabila's Congo, came under fire on Saturday.

An Air France plane carrying 78 people, most of them French citizens, arrived in Paris overnight. Passengers told of looting and violence as well as widespread anti-French sentiment in the former French colony.

"We did not want to leave, as we did not want to lose everything, but it became necessary. We were threatened with knives and machetes because we were French," one man told France Info radio on landing in Paris.
Political parties armed their supporters during ethnic and political fighting which killed 2,000 people following disputed parliamentary elections in 1993.
Fighting in the north between supporters of Sassou Nguesso and former president and prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango, Lissouba's campaign manager, has killed 16 people in under a month.
